sessions.title: Agents-from-zero onboarding (English and Hindi)
sessions.description: Start here if agents are new to you. A beginner-friendly workshop in English and Hindi, run by Dev3pack.

sessions.title: Opening hour: meet and greet and StackChan robot demo
sessions.description: Meet the hub team and the other builders, see the StackChan robot demo, and look at the empty agent stack map on the whiteboard that the sessions all week will fill in.

sessions.title: x402 and ERC-8183: what works today and what is on the roadmap
sessions.description: What each standard is for, what works in production now, and what upstream has not shipped yet. Part of the Standards block.

sessions.title: ERC-8004 in practice: registration works, reputation is the hard part
sessions.description: Identity registries work. Reputation is easy to game, and top-ranked agents often have little product behind them. Part of the Standards block.

sessions.title: Agent payments with real users: three live examples
sessions.description: Three agent payment setups with real users, how to tell them from test traffic, and what builders can copy. Part of the Standards block.

sessions.title: Will agent payments stick?
sessions.description:
Optimists and sceptics argue x402, ERC-8004 and cards, then fill in the whiteboard map with the room. Part of the Standards block.

Moderator: Nicolás Arnedo Villanueva

sessions.title: Follow the money: reading on-chain agent payment data
sessions.description: Agent payment rails keep shipping, but real usage is much smaller than the headlines suggest. Nicolás walks through a practical method for reading on-chain agent payment data: who the actual buyers and sellers are, how to spot repeated counterparties, bot-driven volume and hackathon or test traffic, and what a believable volume number looks like. Then you pair up, pick a chain or facilitator and classify its top payers and sellers as real, bot or test. Part of the Standards block.

sessions.title: Signed Is Not Authorized: a live, bounded user mandate inside an x402 payment
sessions.description: Computing has always tracked what runs, where and how. An agent that pays, signs or decides for you adds a fourth question: on whose authority? Today the answer is a key, and a key cannot tell whether you allow this action now, within these limits. Anantha Krishnan, founder of Sarva Labs and the MOI protocol, shows how authority can be held as live state, and what it looks like when an x402 payment carries a mandate that only the participant can change. Part of the Standards block.

sessions.title: 8004, x402, AP2, ACP and MPP disambiguated, and why not just give the agent a card?
sessions.description: Five agent standards, overlapping names and a lot of confusion. This workshop works from open questions posted by builders. We sort the standards by the job they do (identity, payment or checkout), then walk three common setups: an agent paying for an API, an agent buying from a merchant, and an agent hiring another agent. We close on a question many builders ask: if you can issue an agent a card, why give it a wallet? Part of the Standards block.

sessions.title: Memory your agent owns, with Swarm MCP
sessions.description: Agents need memory, but most keep it in a vendor's database or lose it between sessions. András Arányi (Solar Punk) shows how the Swarm MCP server gives any MCP-compatible agent persistent memory it owns, with a live demo of an agent logbook. Part of the Agent Infra block.

sessions.title: Evidence has a shelf life: queryable, expiring data for ERC-8004 agents
sessions.description: ERC-8004 keeps hashes on-chain but leaves the evidence offchain, with no rule on how long it stays. Arkiv lets agents store validation payloads and coordination state as wallet-owned, queryable data, checked against the on-chain hash and expiring on a set schedule. Part of the Agent Infra block.

sessions.title: Packaged skills that let any agent use a complex protocol correctly
sessions.description: How packaged agent skills give any agent the context it needs to use a complex protocol correctly, with the open-source Swarm skills library as a case study. Part of the Agent Infra block.

sessions.title: Evidence under the payment: who asked, who served, what it cost, signed by both sides
sessions.description: An open-source evidence layer for agent payments on mesh-llm: both sides seal every exchange, paid or not, as a signed, hash-chained record that any third party can verify offline. A 60-second live demo on a running mesh, then hands-on for up to 15 attendees. Part of the Agent Infra block.

sessions.title: Lexon, deterministic AI
sessions.description: Henning Diedrich, creator of Lexon, presents small language models based on symbolic AI, as deterministic as a programming language, and live-codes a hybrid workflow that combines generative and symbolic AI so every step stays transparent. Part of the Agent Infra block.

sessions.title: Networking and agent competition
sessions.description: Meet the other builders, add what you learned to the Bonfires knowledge base with the QR code, and follow the agent competition on the hub TV.

sessions.title: Agents-from-zero onboarding
sessions.description: Start here if agents are new to you. A beginner-friendly workshop run by Dev3pack.

sessions.title: x402 beyond USDC: Paying an agent in USD₮ and USA₮
sessions.description: An agent pays for a service through x402 and the payment settles live on screen, first with a stablecoin, then with USD₮, and USA₮ if live by then. Part of the Payments block.

sessions.title: How x402 settles beyond USDC: permit, ERC-20 and local stablecoins
sessions.description: What adding USD₮ and especially USA₮ means for builders, how settlement works for tokens other than USDC, and how an agent holds funds safely with a self-custodial wallet. Part of the Payments block.

sessions.title: Trust your agent with your card: AgentVault
sessions.description: Where agent card payments stand, how they fit next to x402, and what makes AgentVault different on privacy and security, followed by open discussion on card or x402 for which job. Part of the Payments block.

sessions.title: Pricing and treasury for a machine
sessions.description: How an agent should price and budget in stablecoins. Part of the Payments block.

sessions.title: Price feeds and stablecoin pegs
sessions.description: Where an agent gets a price it can trust, and how price feeds track stablecoin pegs. Part of the Payments block.

sessions.title: USDG on Arbitrum: paying in an ecosystem stablecoin
sessions.description: Paying in an ecosystem stablecoin over x402, with USDG on Arbitrum as the example. Part of the Payments block.

sessions.title: Stablecoins as unit of account: whose money is it?
sessions.description:
Who absorbs a freeze or a depeg when the payer is software, and which currency should an agent price in? A roundtable on issuer risk, freezes and the choice of currency. Part of the Payments block.

Moderator: Nicolás Arnedo Villanueva

sessions.title: Security Risks in x402 Agentic Payments and How to Prevent Them
sessions.description: AI agents can pay for online services using x402. But mistakes can lead to lost money, the same action happening twice, or a service being used without payment. Zuhaib explains five common risks using practical examples and what developers can do to stop abuse and handle failed payments safely. Part of the Payments block.

sessions.title: FX over x402 and shared liquidity
sessions.description: How FX between stablecoins can run inside an x402 payment, using shared liquidity across DEX pools, with a EUR stablecoin in and USDC out. Part of the Payments block.

sessions.title: The last mile into INR and EUR: from stablecoin to local money
sessions.description: Where the rate comes from and what happens at the off-ramp into local money, then the payments block wrap: finishing the Mumbai to Spain payment on the whiteboard. Part of the Payments block.

sessions.title: Giving agents spending power without the keys: self-custodial and permissioned agent wallets
sessions.description: AI agents are starting to pay for things: APIs, compute, each other. The hard part is giving them money without giving them your keys. This session puts three answers side by side. First, an agent with its own self-custodial, multi-chain wallet. Second, a user granting an agent a capped, time-bound, revocable allowance from their own smart account. Third, the account layer underneath: smart accounts, EIP-7702, interop and scaling, and what is still unsolved. Each approach is shown live, followed by a frank comparison of when to use which.

sessions.title: Selling to agents: how an agent finds a service and pays per call
sessions.description: An agent finds a service, gets a quote and pays per call in stablecoins on Celo, with no accounts, API keys or subscriptions, and what that means for selling to agents. Questions and open discussion at the end. Part of the Marketplaces block.

sessions.title: Building agent products with a small team
sessions.description: How agents change the way a small team builds and ships consumer products, and what makes agent features feel simple. Part of the Marketplaces block.

sessions.title: Designing agents that act on real assets
sessions.description: Permissions, visibility and keeping users in control when agents act on real assets. Part of the Marketplaces block.

sessions.title: Your Next Customer Won't Click: Designing for Humans and Agents
sessions.description: Your next customer may arrive as an agent that never opens your homepage. Can it discover your offer, understand the price, get permission and pay, or does your product stop at a login screen? Fortunato examines CLI, API and Markdown as product surfaces, then shows why people still need images, comparisons and clear decisions. Leave knowing what the agent should do, what the human should see and where trust must be earned. Part of the Marketplaces block.

sessions.title: Can an Agent Buy From You? Find, Check, Pay, Get the Result
sessions.description: Can an unfamiliar agent arrive at your service and become a paying customer? Follow an agent from llms.txt to an MCP tool, an ERC-8004 registration check, an x402 payment and a returned result. Then inspect the interface contract: typed inputs, versions, review and rollback. Open discussion with Fortunato at the end. Part of the Marketplaces block.

sessions.title: Networking and agent competition
sessions.description: Meet the other builders, follow the agent competition on the hub TV and try a live x402 payment at the chai vending demo.

sessions.title: Agents-from-zero onboarding
sessions.description: Start here if agents are new to you. A beginner-friendly workshop run by Dev3pack.

sessions.title: What ERC-8004 actually means: identity, reputation and validation in practice
sessions.description: ERC-8004 gives agents an identity, a place for reputation and a way to validate their work. Registering an agent is easy. Making reputation mean something is the hard part. This session walks through the three registries, shows what a real registration looks like, and works through one question: after an agent has paid for a service through x402, can the service provider leave feedback, and how would a reputation network get built from that? The last part is open discussion, plus a hands-on step: register or read an agent on the spot. Part of the Marketplaces block.

sessions.title: Reputation-system failure modes: sybils, review farming, whitewashing
sessions.description: Open agent economies run on reputation, and reputation is the first thing attackers farm. This roundtable maps three classic failure modes: sybil identities minted at machine speed, review farming and wash-traded feedback, and whitewashing, where a bad actor burns an identity and starts fresh. Speakers compare defences across the stack: payment-gated feedback, identity cost and stake, reviewer-weighted scoring, and verifiable evidence kept on durable storage. Part of the Marketplaces block.

sessions.title: How agents find and pay for services
sessions.description: How agents find, trust and pay for a service, with a look at pay-per-call in practice. Part of the Marketplaces block.

sessions.title: Agent communication: A2A, MCP and how agents agree on meaning
sessions.description: MCP and A2A help agents communicate. A successful connection still needs an explicit agreement about what a tool means and returns. Part of the Marketplaces block.

sessions.title: How agents are found by domain, and where identity fits in
sessions.description: How agents are found by domain, and how agent identity fits in. Part of the Marketplaces block.

sessions.title: Agents × UPI: what machine payments can learn from UPI
sessions.description: UPI did not win by being the smartest payment technology. It won because India treated the rail as shared, open public infrastructure and let apps compete on top. Agents now pay for services, pay each other and spend on behalf of people, with no human confirming each step. What should machine payments copy from UPI? Vishnu traces the shared history and principles behind UPI, blockchains and agentic payments, and how UPI reached mass adoption. Piyush covers how authority gets granted: shared rails, interoperability by default, scoped delegation, and mandates that can be changed or revoked in real time. Naina covers what happens after the agent spends: once the PIN is gone, how do we prove a payment matched its mandate, settle disputes, produce receipts that reconcile, and keep payments private but auditable?

sessions.title: Who Gets Sued When the Agent Makes a Mistake? How to get prepared in a decentralized way with KYC and arbitration
sessions.description: An agent buys a service. The payment succeeds. The work is disputed, and nobody can clearly show who authorized the deal. This Agents × Legal Hub session puts one case through the entire chain: the human or company behind the agent, its delegated mandate, the transaction's policy checks, the promised delivery and the remedy when something goes wrong. The room changes the facts: a revoked mandate, an eligible recipient but an unauthorized purpose, or a paid service that fails its specification. Part of the Permissions and Policies block.

sessions.title: Markets Humans Ignore: Economic Mechanisms for AI Agents
sessions.description: Some economic mechanisms look elegant on paper and struggle to attract people: the reward is too small, the task too repetitive, the decision too time-consuming. What changes when the participant is an AI agent? Using prediction markets, curated information and dispute evaluation as examples, Clément examines the cost of participation, the reward for useful work and the consequences of being wrong. Part of the Permissions and Policies block.

sessions.title: Networking and agent competition
sessions.description: Meet the other builders, follow the agent competition on the hub TV and try a live x402 payment at the chai vending demo.

sessions.title: Agents-from-zero onboarding

sessions.title: Machines that pay: robotics and agent payments
sessions.description: What changes when robots and machines pay for things themselves: a community talk on robotics and agent payments.

sessions.title: From discovery to dispute: equip your agent or marketplace to scale
sessions.description: Build the part of your agent business that turns interest into paid work, and a bad experience into a customer you can recover. Bring an agent, API or marketplace idea. We'll pick one and design its complete customer journey on the whiteboard: get discovered through credible profiles, earn trust with verifiable claims and reputation, take x402 payments, define delivery, and handle dissatisfaction through support, refunds and independent dispute resolution. Leave with a customer-flow map, evidence and policy requirements, public code links and one integration you can start building.

sessions.title: Who Answered Your Prompt? The issues in modern inference
sessions.description: When you call an AI API, you're trusting a black box: which model ran, who served it, and whether it was quietly swapped, quantized or censored. This talk unpacks the hidden trust gaps in modern inference and reviews emerging approaches, from cryptographic proofs to decentralized provider networks, for making every answer accountable.

sessions.title: Giving agents authority you can revoke: the Moi layer in action
sessions.description: See how agents act on a user's behalf and how their transactions run via agents on Ethereum, using the Moi authority layer.

sessions.description: The finals of the hub competitions and a wrap-up of the week.

sessions.title: The Oracle Problem for Science + QnA
sessions.description:
In crypto, we often talk about the oracle problem: how do you bring information from the real world onto a blockchain and make a smart contract act on it?DeSci has a much harder version of the same problem. Imagine a research grant that releases funding when a scientific milestone is achieved. What exactly tells the smart contract that the milestone has been achieved
An experiment being completed is not necessarily a successful result. A failed hypothesis can still produce valuable research. Peer review takes time, outcomes are uncertain, and some important scientific progress cannot be reduced to a simple yes or no.X: https://x.com/0xDhruvang, LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/dhruvang-choudhari

sessions.title: Community Context Mapping
sessions.description:
Across the four days of the DeSci Community Hub, we propose using Bonfires, an AI-powered community context and knowledge-mapping platform, to capture insights shared by researchers, builders and attendees through informal discussions, interactive questions and voluntary contributions. On Day 4, we will bring these conversations together in an interactive presentation, exploring a visual knowledge graph of the ideas and connections emerging across the Body, Mind, Heart and Soul themes.
The aim is to demonstrate how collective conversations can become an actionable resource for the community, helping researchers discover one another, identify shared problems and continue building together beyond Devcon. X: https://x.com/sasha_7zee, LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/iqra-sajid71/

sessions.title: EIP content in the new AI-era: why specification clarity matters more than ever
sessions.description: We are all using AIs much more than in the past. We point our AIs to implement specifications, such as EIP documents. These documents are not only used as the root source of truth *now*, but will also be like this in the future. It is therefore even more important that the quality of these documents is as high as possible. Not just for core developers, but also for AIs which implement it, and for the general communication with the public.

sessions.title: The Price Is Right: Setting Gas Prices for Glamsterdam
sessions.description: This talk explores the methodology behind Glamsterdam’s gas repricing work, using EIP-8038 and EIP-2780 to explain how synthetic block testing, cross-client measurements, resource decomposition, and conservative assumptions translate throughput targets into gas costs and shape the final pricing model.

sessions.title: The Agent Economy: Why AI Needs Crypto Rails
sessions.description: AI agents are starting to trade, route liquidity and move real money onchain. Using live perp trading as a case study, this talk shows what agents actually need from crypto rails (permissions, signing, identity and settlement) and where the hype runs ahead of real traction.

sessions.title: Are Confidential Tokens Ready for Enterprise Payments?
sessions.description: ERC-7984 standardizes confidential fungible tokens with encrypted balances and transfer amounts. Drawing on building stablecoin cross-border payment rails at DashX, this talk tests the interface against what enterprise payments need: auditability, selective disclosure, reconciliation and fiat settlement.

sessions.title: Why Your Local-Currency Stablecoin Has No Market
sessions.description: Local-currency stablecoins keep launching, but they can’t scale because their liquidity is too thin and too fragmented to trade on. Using data and case studies from issuers and market makers in Aqua0’s beta, this talk shows where the inefficiencies come from, what they cost, and what it takes to fix them.

sessions.title: Building Trustless Systems, Together
sessions.description: Exploring the tension between human trust and code-based trustlessness in Ethereum, this talk draws on experiences building the ETHCluj community to examine how open collaboration, accountability, and shared ownership can thrive in a rapidly evolving world shaped by AI, privacy, and security challenges.

sessions.title: Token Rights 101 (EN)
sessions.description: Every token makes a claim: ownership, access, a share of cashflow, a vote. This session sets the shared vocabulary for the whole hub. It covers the main rights a token can carry, the mechanisms that create or dilute them (vesting, emissions, vote-escrow, delegation), who can change the rules (admin keys, upgrades), and how rights differ for RWAs & NFTs.

sessions.title: Nobody Votes. Can Better Deliberation Fix It?
sessions.description: Most token holders skip the vote because it costs more time & attention than it returns. Civic tech has been working on the same problem in cities and citizen assemblies, using deliberation tools that find where people agree before anything goes to a vote. This session looks at how those tools work, what they have changed in public decision-making, and what DAOs can borrow from them.

sessions.title: Optimistic Governance: From Vote to Veto
sessions.description: In optimistic governance, a proposal passes by default unless holders object within a set window. The holder’s right shifts from voting yes or no to blocking what they disagree with. That lowers the turnout problem, but it raises new questions: who is watching when nobody votes, how high should the veto bar be, and what stops a team from passing things quietly? This session covers how the model works, where it is already in use, and what holders give up and gain when silence counts as consent.

sessions.description: The evolution of online dispute resolution, the growing role of artificial intelligence in arbitration and mediation, and the importance of maintaining fairness, due process and human judgment while adopting new technologies.

sessions.title: From Pilot to Practice: Lessons From Decentralised Justice in Junin
sessions.description:
Can blockchain-based arbitration handle real-world disputes where public institutions are involved? This session looks at what happens when decentralised dispute resolution moves from theory into practice with governments and institutions. Using the Junin (Argentina) pilot as a case study, we'll cover:
- How cases are scoped, and which disputes suit on-chain resolution
- What changed in process as the pilot moved from design to live cases

sessions.title: Legal and Governance Hub x Agentic Hub Collab: Agents, Authority and Governance
sessions.description: Examines agent transaction liability by tracing a disputed service purchase through its entire chain—covering the principal, delegated mandates, policy checks, verification, and dispute remedies. Designed for market participants, enterprise AI teams, and compliance practitioners.

sessions.title: AI-Art’s Copyright Disputes
sessions.description: This research explores how generative AI models (such as Midjourney, Stability AI, and DALL-E 2) have brought a new wave of intellectual property rights (IPR) disputes to the forefront, categorised primarily into input infringement (unauthorised web-scraping and training on copyrighted artwork) and output infringement (producing content substantially similar to an artist's protected expression). The paper evaluates the insufficiencies of current legal routes (such as expensive and protracted class-action lawsuits) and non-legal tools (like Glaze, Nightshade, and robots.txt files). It then proposes a forward-looking AI Art IPR Dispute Resolution Model in Kleros, integrating decentralised blockchain-based arbitration with Digital Rights Management (DRM) systems.

sessions.title: Who Holds the Keys? Admin Powers, Upgrades & Treasury Drains
sessions.description: A vote or token balance means little if someone else can pause transfers, upgrade the code, mint new tokens or blacklist wallets. This workshop maps who holds each of those powers, what it can change for holders, and what limits it: multisigs, timelocks, expiry and disclosure. We walk through recent treasury drains, where the failure was usually compromised keys & signers rather than broken code. You leave with good practices for teams and a checklist for holders.
